content: H7N2 is a subtype of the Influenza A virus, which is sometimes referred to as the bird flu virus. In 2002, one individual in Virginia, USA, and another in New York, USA, in 2003, were found to have serologic evidence of H7N2 infection. Both individuals fully recovered from the illness. In February 2004, an outbreak of low pathogenic avian influenza (LPAI) A (H7N2) was reported on two chicken farms in Delaware and in four live bird markets in New Jersey that were supplied by the same farms. In March 2004, surveillance samples from a flock of chickens in Maryland tested positive for LPAI H7N2. It is likely that this was the same strain as the one identified in the earlier outbreaks. A study conducted by the CDC following the 2002 outbreaks of H7N2 in commercial poultry farms in western Virginia provided further insights into the virus. On May 24, 2007, an outbreak of H7N2 was confirmed at a poultry farm near Corwen, Wales. This was determined through testing of chickens that had died from H7N2. The owners of the farm in Conwy had purchased 15 Rhode Island Red chickens two weeks prior, but all of these birds succumbed to H7N2. The remaining 32 poultry at the site were culled to prevent further spread of the virus. A one-kilometer exclusion zone was established around the affected property. Within this zone, the movement of birds and bird products was prohibited, and bird gatherings were only permitted under strict licensing conditions. Nine individuals who had been in contact with the infected or deceased poultry and reported flu-like symptoms were tested. Four of these individuals tested positive for evidence of H7N2 infection. They were successfully treated for mild flu symptoms. In early June 2007, it was discovered that the virus had spread to a poultry farm located 70 miles (113 kilometers) away near St. Helens in northwest England. All poultry at this farm were culled, and a one-kilometer exclusion zone was imposed to contain the outbreak.
